title: Petrosian against Spassky, 1966: two exchange sacrifices
outcomes: Tries each of the five decision moments before seeing the move and compares the attempt with the engine's first choice
Says what the usual piece count shows at move 25 (White four points behind) and what the engine at depth 16 rates instead
Points to features of the position on the board, such as the single pawn beside Black's king, that the piece count does not measure, without claiming they alone explain the engine rating
Decides, in a position with a full pawn shelter, that the same exchange sacrifice has no payoff

steps.text: **Petrosian (White) against Spassky (Black)**, game 10 of the 1966 World Championship match in Moscow, 2 May 1966. Both kings castled kingside. In this lesson, the exchange means winning a rook for a bishop or knight, or losing one: you give about five points and get about three, so something on the board must pay the difference. You will play White at five moments and compare your move with the engine's first choice and the game. Engine numbers are evidence at a stated depth, not proof.

steps.caption: Moves 1 to 20. Step through them; the first decision comes at the end.

line.say: White begins with the knight.
White castles; Black castles on the next move.
Pawn takes pawn on f5.
Black's g-pawn recaptures.
The knight goes back to d1.
The bishop goes to b2.
Black's bishop takes the bishop on b2.
White's queen takes it back.
White's g-pawn takes the pawn on f4.
Black's bishop on h3 attacks the rook on f1. Moving it is not forced. What would you lose if the bishop took it and your other rook took back?

steps.caption: 21.Ne3 and the first exchange sacrifice: the engine puts Ne3 first at depth 16, and a rook is given for a bishop.

line.say: The knight goes to e3. The rook on f1 stays attacked.
Black's bishop takes the rook.
White's rook on a1 takes the bishop. A rook has been given for a bishop.
Black's knight goes to g6.

claims.statement: Black's king has one pawn near it: the pawn on h7.

steps.caption: 23.Bg4 Nxf4. Black wins a pawn. At depth 16 the engine rates White about 1.1 pawns up before Bg4.

line.say: The bishop goes to g4, on the diagonal through e6.
Black's knight takes the pawn on f4. It is attacked once and defended once.

claims.statement: After Bg4 exactly two white men attack e6 (the bishop and the pawn on d5).
At depth 16 the engine rates this position between 0.5 and 2 pawns better for White.

steps.caption: 24.Rxf4 Rxf4: the game move, and White has now given up both rooks.

line.say: The rook takes the knight on f4.

What did White get for the two rooks? Black's king has one pawn beside it, Be6+ is coming and White's pieces reach the king while Black's knight on a5 does not. That is the reason; the payoff is the attack, and it is not guaranteed.

claims.statement: At depth 16 the engine rates the position before 24.Rxf4 at least 2.5 pawns better for White.

steps.caption: 25.Be6+ Rf7. Engine numbers are from White's side.

line.say: The bishop gives check from e6.
Black's rook blocks on f7.

claims.statement: Black's king has one pawn near it: the pawn on h7.
At depth 16 the engine rates the position before 25.Be6+ at least 2.5 pawns better for White.

steps.text: **Count it the usual way.** After 25...Rf7, White has 23 points (queen, bishop, two knights, five pawns); Black has 27 (two rooks, queen, knight, five pawns). White is four behind, yet the engine at depth 16 rated the position before 25.Be6+ at least 2.5 pawns better for White. The count only adds up material, not where it stands. You can see Black's king with a single pawn beside it, and Black's knight on a5, far from the kingside. The engine weighs many such features; this lesson names two. Your move.

steps.caption: 26.Ne4 to 29...Rxf7. Step through: the knight takes on d6, then the bishop takes the rook on f7.

line.say: The knight goes to e4 and attacks d6.
Black's queen goes to h4.
The knight takes the pawn on d6.
Black's queen gives check from g5.
The king steps to h1.
Black's rook goes to a7.
The bishop takes the rook on f7 with check.
Black's rook takes the bishop.

claims.statement: After Ne4 exactly one white piece attacks d6 (the knight).

steps.caption: 30.Qh8+. The recorded game ends here with Black resigning. The next board shows the continuation that makes resignation sensible; it was not played.

line.say: The queen goes to h8 with check.
The king takes the queen.

claims.statement: After Qh8+ exactly one black piece attacks the queen on h8 (the king).

steps.caption: The line that follows if Black takes the queen: 31.Nxf7+ forks king and queen. This is the continuation given in secondary sources, not part of the recorded game.

line.say: The knight gives check from f7 and attacks the queen on g5.
The king steps to g7.
The knight takes the queen.

claims.statement: After Nxf7+ Black's only loose piece is the queen on g5.
At depth 16 the engine rates this position at least four pawns better for White.

steps.text: Here the same rook for bishop trade has no payoff, because the king is well covered. The sacrifice depends on the position, not on the move.

**What the game shows.** Skills used: *The exchange sacrifice* (moves 21 and 24), *Piece values depend on the position* (the count said White was behind), *Attacking the castled king* (one pawn beside Black's king) and *Types of sacrifice* (the queen at move 30). At depth 16 the engine's rating climbs from about 1.1 pawns before 23.Bg4 to at least 2.5 before 24.Rxf4, so by the engine's numbers the position changed during moves 21 to 24, well before the last move. Evidence, not proof.

steps.prompt: Which of the five moments (21.Ne3, 23.Bg4, 24.Rxf4, 26.Ne4, 30.Qh8+) would you have missed in a game of your own, and what would you have had to notice to find it?
